title: quic: Handle out-of-order CRYPTO frames, aka "Chaos Protection"
description:
Implement out of order buffering and desegmentation for QUIC
CRYPTO frames. Particularly useful for Chrome's "Chaos Protection"
that intentionally introduces them, but handles out of order
CRYPTO frames in different UDP payloads as well. (Buffering
packets at a higher encryption level until the out of order
lower level frames have arrived is a different issue.)

Adds a preference, which defaults to on since if there is
out of order, it's not very useful to turn it off.

Fix #17732. Fix #18215.

After the latest push the reassembler itself seems fine (other tests are running...) but I found some oddities with the "tree visualization"

In the attached packet, there are 8 CRYPTO frames, but after the last one, the Client Hello seems made by only 2 fragments (because somethings happens after the 7th frame).
I expected to see only one "reassembler tree", after the last CRYPTO frame, with 8 fragments.
Am I wrong?

![Screenshot_from_2022-07-23_10-38-28](/uploads/222c046bb27ee28dd5391380551d51de/Screenshot_from_2022-07-23_10-38-28.png)

[quic_wrong_fragment_tree_anon.pcapng](/uploads/f96bfc25e2788cc00e14ba6fbd4246e2/quic_wrong_fragment_tree_anon.pcapng)

What's happening here is that the behavior is as in [RFC 9001](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9001.html#name-sending-and-receiving-hands)

> TLS is responsible for buffering handshake bytes that have arrived in order. QUIC is responsible for buffering handshake bytes that arrive out of order or for encryption levels that are not yet ready.

The TLS handshake dissector, unlike the subdissectors that run on top of TCP (including the main part of TLS), doesn't report back to whatever called it (like QUIC) with the end offset location of the current PDU. Instead it has its own defragmentation handling that works as long as the bytes are in order.

So what's happening is that those are two separate sets of fragments. First QUIC is doing the out of order processing, and only after it gets the (seventh) fragment of length 108 does it have a completed set of buffered out of order bytes that it sends to the TLS handshake dissector. The TLS handshake dissector examines them and determines that they are a fragment of a Client Hello, so that becomes a handshake fragment.

The next (8th) CRYPTO frame is in order after the previous 7, so it is handed to the TLS dissector immediately, which uses it to complete its pending fragment. The end result is a TLS reassembly made up of two TLS handshake fragments, the first of which is made up of 7 QUIC CRYPTO level fragments.

The approach used with other dissectors that set `pinfo->desegment_len` and `pinfo->desegment_offset` and have the calling dissector (TCP usually) handle everything is more complicated, but is superior not just in the sense of a simpler tree, but also in that if the subdissector determines that we have the start of a PDU and exactly how many additional bytes are needed, and then the caller (TCP or QUIC) receives frames just past the end of that PDU, it can go ahead and start constructing the next PDU after the gap.

That is, the other approach is better in general because (some) gaps can be skipped without stopping dissection, even while doing out of order processing.

However, it's more complicated, would require changes to the TLS dissector as well, and isn't actually very useful for TLS over QUIC because if we don't get the entire handshake we're going to have trouble doing the rest of the dissection. There might be some cases where it is useful and could be done later. (I have some comments to the effect in the code.)

Note that this change doesn't do the last part of that sentence from RFC 9001: If CRYPTO frames for a higher encryption level are received before it's ready (because the lower level handshake isn't finished), they currently are still sent to TLS.
Thanks for the explanation; now it makes sense (to me)

there is a warning with Coverity 

 CID 1507470:    (RESOURCE_LEAK)  >>>     Variable "tmp_key" going out of scope leaks the storage it points to.

I see that, and I don't understand it other than as a false positive. It's created in `pinfo->pool` scope, its members are integers not pointers, and those are copied to an object in file scope if saved.

It goes out of scope in the function, but since it's created the appropriate scope it should be freed when the packet is.

I tried running compiled with Clang and ASAN and it didn't show a new leak.

Yes Coverity don't like pinfo->pool

can you set false positive on Coverity UI ?

+    def check_quic_tls_handshake_reassembly(self, cmd_tshark, capture_file,
+                                       extraArgs=[]):
+        # An assortment of QUIC carrying TLS handshakes that need to be
+        # reassembled, including fragmented in one packet, fragmented in
+        # multiple packets, fragmented in multiple out of order packets,
+        # retried, retried with overlap from the original packets, and retried
+        # with one of the original packets missing (but all data there.)
+        # Include -zexpert just to be sure that nothing Warn or higher occured.
+        # Note level expert infos may be expected with the overlaps and
+        # retransmissions.
+        proc = self.assertRun([cmd_tshark,
+                               '-r', capture_file('quic-fragmented-handshakes.pcapng.gz'),
+                               '-zexpert,warn',
+                               '-Ytls.handshake.type',
+                               '-o', 'gui.column.format:"Handshake Type","%Cus:tls.handshake.type:0:R"',
+                               ] + extraArgs)
+        self.assertEqual(self.countOutput('Client Hello'), 18)
+        self.assertEqual(self.countOutput('Server Hello'), 2)
+        self.assertEqual(self.countOutput('Finished'), 2)
+        self.assertEqual(self.countOutput('New Session Ticket,New Session Ticket'), 1)
+        self.assertEqual(self.countOutput('Certificate'), 2)
+        self.assertFalse(self.grepOutput('Warns'))
+        self.assertFalse(self.grepOutput('Errors'))
+
